items.body:
### What happened?

#134827 (merged 2025-10-23, shipped in client-go v0.36) added two methods to the `cache.Store` interface:

- `Bookmark(rv string)`
- `LastStoreSyncResourceVersion() string`

The package's own test double `cache.FakeCustomStore` (`staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/fake_custom_store.go`) was not updated, so it no longer satisfies `cache.Store`. Downstream test code that passes a `FakeCustomStore` where a `Store` is expected now fails to compile:

```
cannot use &cache.FakeCustomStore{...} (value of type *cache.FakeCustomStore) as cache.Store value:
	*cache.FakeCustomStore does not implement cache.Store (missing method Bookmark)
```

We hit this in the wild during KubeVirt's bump to v0.36.2 (kubevirt/kubevirt#18315) and had to add a local wrapper to keep ~10 test files compiling.

### What did you expect to happen?

`FakeCustomStore` keeps satisfying `cache.Store`. It is named and documented as a general store fake ("lets you define custom functions for store operations") and has satisfied `Store` since 2016. The new narrower `ReflectorStore` interface is not a substitute for read-path consumers (it has no `List`/`GetByKey`), and #134827 carried no deprecation signal for the fake.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
package main

import "k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache"

var _ cache.Store = &cache.FakeCustomStore{} // fails to compile with client-go v0.36.x
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Proposed fix (~15 lines, backward compatible): add `BookmarkFunc func(rv string)` and `LastStoreSyncResourceVersionFunc func() string` fields plus the two delegating methods (no-op / `""` when nil), matching the file's existing pattern. Happy to submit the PR.

### Kubernetes version

client-go v0.36.x (still present on master as of 2026-07-27)

/kind bug

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

items.body:
### What happened?

In our CI environment (Calico Felix functional tests, which start a fresh kube-apiserver per test), a LIST of a CRD hung inside the apiserver for 13+ seconds while identical LISTs from other clients, through the same apiserver, succeeded within 300 ms. The stuck request was still blocked on its first attempt of an etcd KV/Range RPC when the client gave up:

```
{"level":"warn","logger":"etcd-client","caller":"v3@v3.6.5/retry_interceptor.go:65","msg":"retrying of unary invoker failed","target":"etcd-endpoints://0xc004ab9680/[...]:2379","method":"/etcdserverpb.KV/Range","attempt":0,"error":"rpc error: code = Canceled desc = context canceled"}
E ... timeout.go:140] "Post-timeout activity" ... method="GET" path="/apis/crd.projectcalico.org/v1/globalnetworksets"
```

etcd (single node, v3.5.24) was healthy throughout: no slow-apply or read-index warnings, and it served all other requests, including the same LIST from other clients, in milliseconds.

The hung request was the first request ever for that CRD on the freshly started apiserver. First requests trigger lazy creation of the CRD's storage, including a new etcd client (one per CRD - #111476). The hang coincided with a burst of transport churn from ~14 CRD storages being created at once:

```
W ... grpc: addrConn.createTransport failed to connect ... Err: connection error: desc = "error reading server preface: read tcp [...]: use of closed network connection"
W ... grpc: addrConn.createTransport failed to connect ... Err: "transport: failed to write client preface: write tcp [...]: use of closed network connection"
W ... grpc: addrConn.createTransport failed to connect ... Err: "transport: Error while dialing: dial tcp [...]: operation was canceled"
```

### What did you expect to happen?

All requests for that list serviced promptly.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Repeatedly hammer the list CR path on freshly started API server.  It is probabilistic and infrequent.

### Anything else we need to know?

Upstream fix (assuming RCA below is correct)

- grpc/grpc-go#8425 ("Transport close blocks on unresponsive reader"), fixed by grpc/grpc-go#8534 ("transport: Invoke net.Conn.SetReadDeadline in http2_client.Close"), released in grpc-go v1.77.0. Related hardening: grpc/grpc-go#8615 (pickfirstleaf stuck in IDLE), released in v1.76.0.
- Neither was backported to grpc-go 1.72.x.
- kubernetes master picked up the fix incidentally via routine dependency maintenance (#136227, grpc v1.78.0; then #137906, v1.79.3), so 1.36 is fixed. release-1.35 (through v1.35.7) and release-1.34 still vendor grpc-go v1.72.2.

Potential root cause (from Claude): 

internal/transport/http2_client.go strands in-flight RPCs when a transport leaves service:

- Close(): calls t.onClose(...) first the subchannel immediately reports the transport dead and new RPCs move to a fresh transport — then waits for GOAWAY write, then blocks on <-t.readerDone with no deadline, and only after that errors the in-flight streams. If the dying connection goes mute (no FIN/RST reaches the reader), in-flight streams wait indefinitely.
- GracefulClose(): calls t.onClose(...) and then waits for active streams to drain with no deadline; in-flight streams are never errored at all.

So an RPC that lands on a transport just as it is being recycled is stranded on attempt 0: the etcd retry interceptor never sees the attempt finish, so it never retries, while every new RPC succeeds on the replacement transport. The etcd client defaults to WaitForReady(true), so nothing bounds the attempt client-side. The only recovery paths are the etcd client keepalive configured in storagebackend/factory/etcd3.go (30s ping / 10s timeout → ~40–86s) or the HTTP request's own context ending (server --request-timeout, or the caller disconnecting — which is what we observed).

Two things make first-requests-to-CRDs a reliable trigger window: per-CRD lazy storage creation churns subchannels exactly when the request is issued, and with ResilientWatchCacheInitialization a LIST arriving before the CRD's watch cache is ready delegates straight to etcd (cacher/delegator.go), putting the user request directly on the brand-new transport.

Caveat: the chain above is established from the logs plus reading the vendored code; we have not reproduced it with a patched grpc-go to bisect.

items.body:
The e2e test framework has several patterns that cause flakiness, silent resource leaks, and hard-to-debug failures, especially in disruptive tests that restart API servers or control plane components. PR 137832 addresses these across 13 files (185 additions, 41 deletions), touching SIG api-machinery, apps, cloud-provider, network, node, storage, and testing.

Error suppression hides resource leaks. Across the test suite, cleanup code discards errors from Delete calls. In test/e2e/apimachinery/aggregator.go, the cleanupSampleAPIServer function has 10 such calls (APIService, Deployment, Secret, Service, ServiceAccount, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding, ClusterRole) all silently swallowed. Same pattern in test/e2e/apimachinery/apply.go (4 deployments/pods), test/e2e/apps/rc.go (DeleteCollection), and test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go (ConfigMaps in defer blocks). When these fail, resources leak into subsequent tests with zero trace of what went wrong.

No retry on transient API server errors. GetControlPlaneNodes in test/e2e/framework/util.go calls Nodes().List() and immediately fails on any error. During disruptive tests (daemon restarts, etcd failure injection), the API server is expected to be briefly unreachable. The same issue exists in allNodesReady at test/e2e/framework/node/helper.go and RestartNodes at test/e2e/common/util.go. A transient connection refused or 503 kills the entire test instead of retrying. The fix introduces IsRetryableAPIError which checks for connection refused/reset, server timeout, 429, 503, 500, and unexpected server errors, plus a new WaitForControlPlaneNodes that wraps the listing in a polling loop with retry-on-transient logic.

Healthz returns 200 before daemon is ready. RestartDaemonConfig.waitUp in test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go considers the daemon ready when /healthz returns HTTP 200. After a kubelet restart, the health endpoint can report ok while kubelet is still recovering. Logs show errors, pods are not yet scheduled. The fix adds verifyDaemonReadiness which SSHes into the node and checks the last 20 lines of /var/log/kubelet.log for error patterns before declaring readiness.

Goroutines not gracefully stopped. In test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go, a cache.NewInformer controller is started with go controller.Run(backgroundCtx.Done()). The cleanup calls cancel() but does not wait for the controller goroutine to finish. The fix replaces this with a dedicated stopCh channel and DeferCleanup that closes the channel then sleeps 100ms to allow graceful shutdown.

PVC deletion races with pod references. DeleteAllStatefulSets in test/e2e/framework/statefulset/rest.go has a TODO comment about not checking whether pods still reference PVCs before deleting them. The current code deletes PVCs immediately, which can fail or leave orphaned PVs when pods are still running. The fix lists pods, checks volume references, and only deletes PVCs that are not in use, with foreground propagation.

Duplicated control plane filtering. GetControlPlaneNodes and WaitForControlPlaneNodes both contain the same node filtering logic (check for control-plane label and NoSchedule taint). The second commit extracts this into a shared filterControlPlaneNodes helper.

All changes are in e2e test code, no user-facing impact.

Related issues:
- 109600: prevent the Expect(err).NotTo(HaveOccurred()) and ExpectNoError(err) anti-pattern in e2e tests (same category of error handling problems)
- 86253: sample-apiserver returns error instead of falling back to second Accept type (directly affects the aggregator.go test modified in this PR)
- 135285: GOAWAY are not handled gracefully in apiserver when aggregating (related network error handling)
- 105536: Orphaned pod found, but error not a directory occurred when trying to remove the volumes dir (related resource cleanup issue)

items.title: APF queueset can panic ("slice bounds out of range") and crash the apiserver when a queue holding a lingering request is removed after a DesiredNumQueues reduction

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?

In `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/flowcontrol/fairqueuing/queueset/queueset.go`, a request that has finished its main service but still occupies seats during its `AdditionalLatency` (a "lingering" request, e.g. a mutating request whose work estimate reserves seats for its watch fan-out) is removed from `requestsExecuting` immediately in `finishRequestLocked`, while releasing its seats and calling `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked` is deferred to an `EventAfterDuration` callback that fires `AdditionalLatency` later.

`removeQueueIfEmptyLocked` decides whether to drop an excess queue using:

```go
if len(qs.queues) > qs.qCfg.DesiredNumQueues &&
    r.queue.requestsWaiting.Length() == 0 &&
    r.queue.requestsExecuting.Len() == 0 {   // does not check seatsInUse
    qs.queues = removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes(qs.queues, r.queue.index)
    ...
}
```

It does not check `seatsInUse`. So if `DesiredNumQueues` has been reduced (excess queues draining by attrition) and a queue Q holds a lingering request `r` plus another request `s`, then when `s` finishes it sees Q as empty (0 waiting, 0 executing — `r` was already removed from the executing set) and removes Q, even though `r`'s seats still linger. `removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes` only fixes up the `index` field of the *kept* queues, so the removed Q keeps a now-stale `index`, and `r.queue` still points at it. When `r`'s lingering timer later fires, its deferred `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked(r)` calls `removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes(qs.queues, <stale index>)` a second time:

- if the stale index is out of range for the now-shorter slice, `queues[index+1:]` panics with `slice bounds out of range`;
- otherwise it removes a different, live queue, silently corrupting fairness/seat accounting and stranding that flow's requests.

The panic runs in the goroutine spawned by `eventclock.Real.EventAfterDuration` (`go func(){ t := <-ch; f(t) }()`), which has no `recover`, so it crashes the whole apiserver process.

### What did you expect to happen?

The queue should not be removed while a lingering request still holds seats in it, and it should never be removed twice.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Unit-level, with the queueset's fake event clock (test in `package queueset`):

1. Build a queuing queueset with `DesiredNumQueues: 3, HandSize: 1` and ample concurrency.
2. `StartRequest` two requests with the same hash (so they share queue index 2): `r` with `WorkEstimate{InitialSeats:1, FinalSeats:1, AdditionalLatency: time.Second}` (lingering) and `s` normal.
3. Reconfigure to `DesiredNumQueues: 1` (the three queues remain, draining by attrition).
4. `r.Finish(...)` then `s.Finish(...)`.
5. Advance the fake clock past `AdditionalLatency`.

Result on current master: `panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [3:2]` in `removeQueueAndUpdateIndexes`, from the lingering timer callback. (A regression test is attached; it panics before the fix and passes after.)


### Anything else we need to know?

Trigger requires an operator to reduce a PriorityLevelConfiguration's `queuing.queues` (so excess queues are draining) together with the right concurrent traffic and timing, so probability is low; but the consequence (apiserver panic, or silent fairness corruption) is severe, and it is reachable through supported configuration. This is a robustness bug on configuration change, not a security issue (no unprivileged trigger, no escalation).

Fix: add `&& r.queue.seatsInUse == 0` to the `removeQueueIfEmptyLocked` guard so a queue is not removed while a lingering request still holds its seats; the queue is then removed exactly once, by the lingering request's own deferred call after its seats are released.

### Kubernetes version

Current master (aa94f417962)

N/A (apiserver unit-level).

items.title: CRD with identical per-version selectableFields but differing per-version schemas is rejected due to internal hoisting

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?

Creating a multi-version `apiextensions.k8s.io/v1` CRD that declares the **same** `selectableFields` on two served versions whose **schemas differ** is rejected by the apiserver:

```
The CustomResourceDefinition "widgets.example.com" is invalid:
spec.selectableFields: Invalid value: "": may only be set when validations.schema is included
```

The error is doubly confusing: the manifest sets only `spec.versions[*].selectableFields` (valid per the v1 API), yet the error references top-level `spec.selectableFields` — a field that does not exist in the v1 API the user submitted.

**Root cause (from reading the source):** `Convert_v1_CustomResourceDefinitionSpec_To_apiextensions_CustomResourceDefinitionSpec` (`staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/v1/conversion.go`) hoists each of the four per-version fields (`subresources`, `schema`, `additionalPrinterColumns`, `selectableFields`) to the internal top-level spec **independently**, whenever that field is identical across all versions. So with identical `selectableFields` but differing schemas:

- `selectableFields` **is** hoisted to internal `spec.SelectableFields` (and cleared per-version),
- `schema` is **not** hoisted (internal `spec.Validation` stays nil),

and internal validation then rejects the combination the conversion itself created (top-level `selectableFields` requires a top-level `validations.schema`). The user's input was never invalid; the independent hoisting manufactured the invalid internal state.

### What did you expect to happen?

Per-version `selectableFields` to be accepted on any served version, independent of whether the other versions' schemas are identical. KEP-4358 field selectors are declared per-version in v1; whether two versions happen to share a schema should not change the validity of identical selector declarations.

**Real-world impact:** any multi-version CRD mid-graduation — the standard pattern of serving two versions where the newer one drops deprecated fields — cannot offer the same field selector on both served versions. We hit this graduating a CRD whose new version removes two deprecated fields; controllers watching via field selector on the old version could not keep the selector when the new version was added. Workarounds: declare `selectableFields` on only one version (losing field selectors on the others), or keep the version schemas byte-identical (defeating the point of graduation).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply this CRD:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: widgets.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: widgets
    singular: widget
    kind: Widget
    listKind: WidgetList
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    selectableFields:
    - jsonPath: .spec.name
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              name: {type: string}
              extra: {type: string}   # <- v1-only field: schemas differ
  - name: v2
    served: true
    storage: false
    selectableFields:
    - jsonPath: .spec.name
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              name: {type: string}
```

→ rejected with the error above.

Control matrix (verified against kube-apiserver v1.35.0):

| per-version schemas | selectableFields | result |
|---|---|---|
| differ | on one version only | accepted |
| differ | identical on both | **rejected** |
| identical | identical on both | accepted (both hoist together) |

The identical-schemas row confirms the failure is the hoisting *interaction*, not the field declarations themselves.

### Anything else we need to know?

Possible fixes:

- Couple the hoisting: hoist `selectableFields` (and `additionalPrinterColumns`/`subresources`) only when `schema` is also hoisted; or
- Relax the spec validation to accept internal top-level `selectableFields` without a top-level schema when every version carries a schema.

Either preserves round-tripping while accepting the valid v1 input. Independent of the fix, the error message would benefit from mentioning that identical per-version declarations can trigger it, since `spec.selectableFields` is not settable in the v1 API.

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

items.title: CEL map-list concatenation preserves duplicate new keys from the right operand

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?

Schema-aware CEL map-list concatenation keeps duplicate new keys from the right operand instead of merging them.

`addToMapList` builds an index for the left operand, but does not add a key to that index when it appends the first new element from the right operand. A later element with the same key is therefore appended again.

For a map list keyed by `key1,key2`, if `x.mapList` contains two existing entries, this expression currently produces four entries and preserves both values `9` and `10`:

```cel
x.mapList + [
  {'key1': 'new', 'key2': 'key', 'value': 9},
  {'key1': 'new', 'key2': 'key', 'value': 10},
]
```

This breaks the merge-by-key semantics implemented for `x-kubernetes-list-type: map`. CEL policies that construct or inspect associative lists can observe the wrong size/value. Mutation expressions can also emit duplicate map keys, causing the admission request to be rejected instead of applying the later value.

### What did you expect to happen?

The first new key from the right operand should be appended and indexed. A later element with that key should overwrite it in place, so the example has one `new,key` entry with value `10`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add this case to `TestListAdd` in `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/cel/common/values_test.go` using the existing `x.mapList` fixture:

```go
{
    name: "map list + literal list merges duplicate new keys",
    expression: "size(x.mapList + [{'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 9}, {'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 10}]) == 3 && (x.mapList + [{'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 9}, {'key1': 'k1v9', 'key2': 'k2v9', 'value': 10}])[2].value == 10",
}
```

Then run:

```console
GOWORK=off go test ./pkg/cel/common -run TestListAdd -count=1
```

The case fails with `Expected true with typed values but got false` on current `master`.

### Anything else we need to know?

The behavior is in the map-list concatenation support merged by #140292. Updating `keyToIdx` immediately after appending a new key fixes the regression and makes the test pass.

items.body:
### What happened?

Creating a `StorageVersionMigration` for a resource, then removing that resource from the cluster (e.g. deleting the CRD) while the migration is still pending, makes the `kube-controller-manager` panic and enter `CrashLoopBackOff`.

The storage-version-migrator controller's `sync` dereferences a nil `*schema.GroupVersionResource`:

```
E0714 13:08:33 "Observed a panic" panic="runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference"
	k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator.(*SVMController).sync(...)
		pkg/controller/storageversionmigrator/storageversionmigrator.go:227
...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked]
```

In `sync`, `resourceFor` returns `(nil, false, nil)` when the resource is not in the RESTMapper (this is the normal "unknown resource" return, not an error), and the following line logs `gvr.String()` on that nil pointer:

```go
gvr, exists, err := resourceFor(svmc.restMapper, toBeProcessedSVM.Spec.Resource)
if err != nil { return err }
if !exists {
    logger.V(4).Info("resource does not exist in our rest mapper", "gvr", gvr.String()) // gvr is nil -> panic
    ...
}
```

`GroupVersionResource.String()` has a value receiver, so calling it on a nil pointer dereferences it. The arguments of `logger.V(4).Info(...)` are evaluated unconditionally, so this happens regardless of the log verbosity. The panic crashes the whole controller-manager (all controllers stop) until the offending `StorageVersionMigration` is removed.

Note: the sibling function in the same package (`ResourceVersionController.sync` in `resourceversion.go`) handles the exact same `!exists` case without touching `gvr`, which is what makes this look like an oversight.

### What did you expect to happen?

The controller should handle a missing resource gracefully (it already intends to: it requeues for up to one minute, then marks the migration failed) without panicking or crashing the controller-manager.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a cluster with the `StorageVersionMigrator` feature enabled and the `storagemigration.k8s.io/v1beta1` API served:

```bash
# 1. A CRD (migrating a CRD to a new storage version is a documented use case)
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata: {name: widgets.example.com}
spec:
  group: example.com
  names: {plural: widgets, singular: widget, kind: Widget, listKind: WidgetList}
  scope: Namespaced
  versions: [{name: v1, served: true, storage: true, schema: {openAPIV3Schema: {type: object}}}]
YAML

# 2. Request a storage version migration for that resource
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: storagemigration.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: StorageVersionMigration
metadata: {name: migrate-widgets}
spec: {resource: {group: example.com, resource: widgets}}
YAML

# 3. Delete the CRD (it leaves the RESTMapper) while the migration is pending
kubectl delete crd widgets.example.com
```

Within ~30-60s the kube-controller-manager panics and goes into CrashLoopBackOff:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-controller-manager   # restartCount increasing, CrashLoopBackOff
kubectl -n kube-system logs <kcm-pod> --previous | grep -A2 "nil pointer"
```

Removing the `StorageVersionMigration` (`kubectl delete storageversionmigration migrate-widgets`) lets the controller-manager recover.

A unit-level reproduction (fake client, no cluster) is also available if you want it.

### Anything else we need to know?

Root cause is a single line (`gvr.String()` on a nil pointer). Trigger requires cluster-admin rights (StorageVersionMigration is cluster-scoped) plus the target resource disappearing from the RESTMapper, so this is not a privilege-escalation issue, but the crash takes down the entire controller-manager.

I have a fix ready (a one-line change: log the migration's `spec.resource` instead of the nil `gvr`) plus a regression test that panics without the fix and passes with it, and I'm happy to open a PR.

items.title: utilyaml: YAMLReader/YAMLOrJSONDecoder corrupts UTF-16 input, causing misleading "yaml: incomplete UTF-16 character"

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: needs-triage

items.body:
/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

### What happened?

`k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml.YAMLOrJSONDecoder` (via the underlying `YAMLReader`/`LineReader`) corrupts UTF-16 encoded input: a valid, BOM'd UTF-16 LE YAML document comes out of `YAMLReader.Read()` one byte longer than it went in — an odd-length UTF-16 stream — and the downstream yaml parser then fails with `yaml: incomplete UTF-16 character`. The error blames the user's file for being truncated when the file is actually valid; the truncation is introduced by the reader itself.

The yaml parser is not at fault: go-yaml is a libyaml port and handles BOM'd UTF-16 natively — `yaml.v2`, `yaml.v3` and `sigs.k8s.io/yaml` all parse the same bytes fine when handed the unmangled stream.

The corruption is in `LineReader.Read()`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/v0.36.2/pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go#L447-L461

`bufio.Reader.ReadLine()` (L456) splits at the raw `0x0a` byte — a UTF-8 assumption — and strips it, then `buffer.WriteByte('\n')` (L459) re-appends a *single-byte* UTF-8 newline. Mid-stream this happens to round-trip: each two-byte `0a 00` newline loses its `0a` to `ReadLine`, gains a fresh `0a` from `WriteByte`, and the orphaned `00` leads the next line, so the bytes reassemble in order. But at EOF the orphaned final `00` comes back as one more "line" and gets its own appended `0a`, so the stream grows by one byte and every subsequent UTF-16 code unit boundary is intact except the total length is now odd. A 314-byte document exits the reader as 315 bytes ending `... 0a 00 0a`.

This is byte-for-byte the encoding Windows PowerShell 5.1 produces with a plain `>` redirect, so "I wrote a manifest on Windows and the controller says my YAML is broken" is the practical failure mode.

### What did you expect to happen?

One of:

- BOM-detected UTF-16 input parses successfully. There is 10-year-old precedent for exactly this: kubectl has transcoded UTF-16 at the file-reading layer since 2016 (#39008), and still does — https://github.com/kubernetes/cli-runtime/blob/master/pkg/resource/visitor.go#L558-L561 wraps every file in `unicode.BOMOverride(unicode.UTF8.NewDecoder())` before the decoder sees it. That protection lives only in cli-runtime's `FileVisitor`; every other consumer of `YAMLOrJSONDecoder`/`YAMLReader` (controllers, operators, anything decoding user-supplied streams) is exposed.
- Or an early, explicit error ("unsupported encoding: UTF-16; convert to UTF-8") instead of silent corruption plus a misleading parser error.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Encode any valid manifest as UTF-16 LE with BOM (what PowerShell `echo ... > file.yaml` writes):

```console
$ { printf '\xff\xfe'; iconv -f UTF-8 -t UTF-16LE svc.yaml; } > svc-utf16.yaml
```

```go
package main

import (
	"bufio"
	"bytes"
	"fmt"
	"os"

	utilyaml "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml"
)

func main() {
	data, _ := os.ReadFile("svc-utf16.yaml")

	var out map[string]interface{}
	err := utilyaml.NewYAMLOrJSONDecoder(bytes.NewReader(data), 4096).Decode(&out)
	fmt.Println("Decode err:", err)

	r := utilyaml.NewYAMLReader(bufio.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(data)))
	chunk, _ := r.Read()
	fmt.Printf("reader in: %d bytes, out: %d bytes\n", len(data), len(chunk))
}
```

Output (apimachinery v0.36.2):

```
Decode err: error converting YAML to JSON: yaml: incomplete UTF-16 character
reader in: 314 bytes, out: 315 bytes
```

The same file parses fine with `sigs.k8s.io/yaml.Unmarshal` directly, and with `kubectl apply -f` (thanks to the cli-runtime transcoder).

### Anything else we need to know?

Real-world sighting: this is the root cause of fluxcd/flux2#1126 (2021) — kustomize-controller validated user manifests through kustomize's legacy `kunstruct` factory, which delegates to `NewYAMLOrJSONDecoder`, and PowerShell-authored files failed with this exact error. Full RCA with byte traces: https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/issues/1126#issuecomment-4967789882. Flux escaped by rewriting its generator, but the trap remains armed for any other consumer.

Verified present in v0.20.2 through v0.36.2; `LineReader` is unchanged on master.

Happy to send a PR. Two possible directions — transcode on BOM detection at `YAMLReader`/`YAMLOrJSONDecoder` entry (can be done with stdlib `unicode/utf16`, no new dependency, mirroring what cli-runtime does with `x/text`), or reject non-UTF-8 input early with a clear error. Whichever SIG API Machinery prefers.

### Kubernetes version

N/A — library bug in `k8s.io/apimachinery` (verified v0.20.2 → v0.36.2, master unchanged).

### Cloud provider

N/A

### OS version

In 2025 I fixed several watch client shutdown bugs: #131266 (reflector Stop deadlock), #131321 (VeryShortWatchError), #131706 (watch test body cleanup). Thanks again to @wojtek-t and @liggitt for those reviews.

The test work in #131505 turned up three more bugs. They were documented there as TODOs but never fixed. I've verified all three still exist on master (843726939e9) and plan to send one small PR per bug:

1. **Response body leak.** `Request.Watch` doesn't close `resp.Body` when content-type negotiation fails. Tracked in #140464.

2. **Error event after Stop.** `StreamWatcher.receive` selects between the done channel and the error send. When both are ready Go picks at random, so a decode error racing with `Stop()` reaches the consumer about half the time. First reported back in 2015 (#6433) and again recently in #139782. The open fix #139783 adds the http2 error string to `IsProbableEOF`, which helps that case, but the race allows any decode error through after Stop. My PR will check the done channel first so a stopped watcher just closes its result channel.

3. **Broken error unwrapping.** `StreamWatcher.receive` and the client watch decoder wrap decode errors with `%v`, which severs `errors.Is`/`errors.As`. Consumers end up string-matching the message. Config Sync, for example, matches the literal "unable to decode an event from the watch stream: context canceled" text to detect shutdown. Small enough to fix without its own issue.

Each PR is small, structured as a failing test commit followed by the fix, with race detector and stress output in the description.

Requesting `/triage accepted` so the fix PRs land against accepted issues.

items.body:
## Summary

For `DeviceAllocationModeExactCount`, the device request `Count` is an `int64` and is currently validated only for its lower bound.

Both `ExactDeviceRequest.Count` and `DeviceSubRequest.Count` flow through `validateDeviceAllocationMode`:

```go
case resource.DeviceAllocationModeExactCount:
    if count <= 0 {
        allErrs = append(allErrs,
            field.Invalid(countFldPath, count, "must be greater than zero"))
    }
```

There is no upper bound, so the API accepts the entire positive `int64` range, including:

```text
9223372036854775807
```

I verified this behavior against Kubernetes v1.36.1.

This issue is not asserting that every positive `int64` value is invalid, nor that Kubernetes itself must necessarily impose a small device-count limit. The question is whether the API should define a practical upper bound, or at least explicitly document an overflow-safety contract for consumers.

## Motivation

Several independent DRA consumers have treated `Count` as an ordinary device quantity and aggregated or multiplied it using unchecked `int64` arithmetic.

Because one request may contain `math.MaxInt64`, even two requests are sufficient to wrap a running sum negative.

I audited three independent scheduler and quota-accounting codebases, and each had independently written unchecked `int64` aggregation of `Count`. To be clear, the reports and fixes below are all mine, so this is one audit across three projects rather than three separate discoveries. The point is that three separately maintained codebases each missed the same thing:

| Project                     | Observed path                                                            | Current status                                     |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| kubernetes-sigs/kueue       | Per-DeviceClass DRA quota count; two `MaxInt64` requests wrapped to `-2` | #12896, fixed through #12897 and related hardening |
| volcano-sh/volcano          | Device count addition, gang-size multiplication, and quota comparison    | #5621; release-1.15 backport #5626 merged          |
| kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler | GPU count accumulation into queue and parent fair-share accounting       | reported in #1873; fix #1874 under discussion      |

In the reproduced Kueue and KAI cases, the oversized requests did not result in real device allocation or resource theft. The requests were impossible to satisfy, and no cross-tenant resource escalation was demonstrated.

On the KAI fix specifically, a maintainer has reasonably questioned whether it is worth the added complexity given the trigger is currently unreachable. That is a fair question, and it is exactly the kind of call that becomes easier to make once the API states its intended contract, which is what this issue asks for.

The observed impact is therefore accounting integrity and robustness:

* negative quota or fair-share values;
* an impossible workload being admitted by an out-of-tree quota layer;
* corrupted queue accounting while the workload remains pending;
* additional defensive fixes being needed independently in multiple consumers.

This is a low-severity correctness and API-contract issue, not a security report.

## Why unschedulability does not fully contain the problem

A request for `math.MaxInt64` devices cannot be satisfied by a real cluster.

However, the affected out-of-tree implementations process and aggregate the request while it is still pending, before successful device allocation or node binding. Therefore, the fact that no node can satisfy the request does not prevent the request from corrupting quota or fair-share bookkeeping.

No equivalent overflow in an in-tree scheduler or allocator path has been demonstrated here. The confirmed impact so far is in out-of-tree consumers.

## Current API contract

DRA already places explicit limits on several collection sizes, such as the number of devices in an individual `ResourceSlice`, counter sets, counters, selectors, and subrequests.

Those limits are not directly equivalent to a semantic limit on the total number of devices requested, and other DRA scalar `int64` fields are also not necessarily upper-bounded.

Therefore, the absence of an upper bound on `Count` is not by itself proof of a validation bug.

Notably, the in-tree structured allocator explicitly guards this exact-count path and comments on it directly (`dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`):

```go
case resourceapi.DeviceAllocationModeExactCount:
    numDevices := request.count()
    if numDevices > math.MaxInt {
        // Allowed by API validation, but doesn't make sense.
        return requestData, fmt.Errorf("... exact count %d is too large", ...)
    }
```

That check is a cast-safety guard before `int(numDevices)`; on a 64-bit platform `math.MaxInt == math.MaxInt64`, so it is a no-op for the values here. What actually protects the in-tree allocator is that it draws from a bounded pool of real devices, so an impossible count simply fails to allocate. Out-of-tree quota and fair-share accounting has no such natural bound and sums the counts directly, which is why the same input wraps their books negative. The concern is recognized in-tree (the comment says as much), but only implicitly, and the consumers that most need the contract are precisely the ones without the pool's protection.

The recurring downstream failures instead suggest that the intended arithmetic contract is currently too easy for consumers to miss:

* Is the full positive `int64` range intentionally valid?
* Must all consumers use checked or saturating addition and multiplication?
* Or should obviously impossible counts be rejected at the API boundary?

## Possible approaches

### A. Document the full-range contract and audit consumers

Keep the field unbounded, but update the API godoc and DRA documentation to state explicitly that:

* `Count` may contain any positive `int64` value;
* consumers must treat it as untrusted input;
* additions and multiplications must use checked or saturating arithmetic;
* unschedulability must not be relied upon to protect accounting code.

This is compatible and makes the intended responsibility clear.

It may also be useful to audit in-tree consumers for unchecked aggregation, even though no in-tree overflow has been demonstrated in this report.

### B. Add a practical API upper bound

Define and validate a maximum device count, similar in form to other DRA validation constants.

This would reject obviously impossible requests at the source and reduce the range that every consumer must handle.

However:

* the maximum requires a defensible semantic justification;
* this changes validation for an existing API field;
* compatibility treatment for already stored objects requires SIG API Machinery review;
* the relevant native-type declarative-validation work is KEP-5073, not CRD validation ratcheting under KEP-4008;
* a per-request upper bound does not eliminate the need for checked arithmetic when counts are multiplied or aggregated across claims and pods.

### C. Do both

Document that consumers must always use overflow-safe arithmetic, while separately considering a practical API bound as defense in depth.

This avoids treating validation as a replacement for safe consumer arithmetic.

## What I'm asking

To keep this concrete and small: would SIG Node accept a short godoc note on `Count` (and `DeviceSubRequest.Count`) stating that it is unbounded up to `MaxInt64`, that consumers must aggregate and multiply it with overflow-safe arithmetic, and that unschedulability must not be relied on to protect accounting code? I am happy to open that PR.

A hard API upper bound (approach B) is a larger, separate question: it changes validation on a GA field and would need a KEP plus SIG API Machinery review, so I am not proposing it here. Whether in-tree consumers should also be audited is likewise secondary and can be split out.

/sig node
/wg device-management
/kind feature

labels.name: sig/api-machinery

labels.description: Issues or PRs related to API validation and declarative validation

items.body:
### What happened?

Currently, many update validation methods in the codebase call their corresponding create validation methods. This pattern results in `ValidateObjectMeta` (and by extension `ValidateObjectMetaDeclaratively(Create, ...)`) being called during an update validation pass.

This has two main negative consequences:
1. It will break any future ratcheting of metadata.
2. It causes redundant validation, as `ValidateObjectMetaDeclaratively` may be called multiple times during the update pass (once explicitly for the update, and once implicitly via the create validation method).

### Example

In `staging/src/k8s.io/kube-aggregator/pkg/apis/apiregistration/validation/validation.go` during PR #139505:
```go
func ValidateAPIServiceUpdate(ctx context.Context, newAPIService *apiregistration.APIService, oldAPIService *apiregistration.APIService) field.ErrorList {
	allErrs := validation.ValidateObjectMetaDeclaratively(ctx, operation.Update, &newAPIService.ObjectMeta, &oldAPIService.ObjectMeta, false, nil, field.NewPath("metadata"), utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(features.DeclarativeValidationBeta))
	allErrs = append(allErrs, ValidateAPIService(ctx, newAPIService)...) // <-- Calls create validation
	// ...
```

As noted by @lalitc375 in `https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139505#discussion_r3546302067`, this pattern is very common in the validation code for native types. Most of the update validation methods call the create validations method, which in turn calls `ValidateObjectMeta`.

### Action Item

We need to solve this problem horizontally across the codebase to ensure update validation passes only run update-specific logic and do not inadvertently trigger create-specific validations.

_Originally raised by @jpbetz in [kubernetes/kubernetes#139505 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139505#discussion_r3540859399)_

labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

labels.description: Issues or PRs related to API validation and declarative validation

items.body:
**Description:**

`+k8s:monotonic` validation marker enforces that integer fields are non-decreasing during updates. However, a monotonic marker alone is not sufficient to guarantee monotonicity. To prevent API design flaws where a monotonic field can be reset or bypass decrease prevention checks, we need to enforce the correct combination of markers.

**Proposed linter rule:**

Any field marked with `+k8s:monotonic` :
- Must have a `+k8s:minimum` marker to prevent it from being initialised with or set to negative values.
- Must be marked with `+k8s:required` or if it is optional, it must explicitly prevent unsetting during updates by `+k8s:update=NoUnset`

To implement this, the kube-api-linter must be updated to support matching specific tag values in the `dependenttags` linter (e.g. recognize `dependsOn: +K8s:update=NoUnset` instead of just key-level matches).

As suggested https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137881#discussion_r3540568171

items.title: kube-apiserver 1.35+ never shuts down on SIGTERM when its identity Lease cannot be created (e.g. hostname longer than 63 bytes)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?

On hosts with hostnames longer than 63 bytes, `kube-apiserver` does not shut down after `SIGTERM`. It keeps serving until `SIGKILL`.

This reproduces consistently with official v1.35.0 and v1.36.2 binaries on Linux and macOS. v1.34 shuts down normally on the same hosts.

The hostname matters because the apiserver identity Lease is labeled with `kubernetes.io/hostname`, and Kubernetes label values are limited to 63 bytes. When the hostname exceeds that limit, Lease creation is rejected forever. Since v1.35, shutdown waits on that retry loop, causing a deadlock.

The retry loop logs:

```
    E0705 16:05:59 controller.go:201] "Failed to ensure lease exists, will retry"
    err="Lease.coordination.k8s.io \"apiserver-...\" is invalid: metadata.labels:
    Invalid value: \"sat12-dp146-...-FE94C5DD19A3.local\":
    must be no more than 63 bytes" interval="7s"
```
A goroutine dump after `SIGTERM` shows the shutdown hook blocked in `Stop()` while the lease controller is still retrying:

```
    goroutine 1 [sync.Mutex.Lock]:
    k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease.(*controller).Stop(...)
            k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go:131
    k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controlplane/apiserver.completedConfig.New.func10()
            k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/controlplane/apiserver/server.go:279
    k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server.(*GenericAPIServer).RunPreShutdownHooks(...)

    goroutine 3459 [select]:
    k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease.(*controller).backoffEnsureLease(...)
            k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go:203
    k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease.(*controller).sync(...)
            k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller.go:174
```

The deadlock is:

1. `sync()` holds `reconcilingLock` and calls `backoffEnsureLease(ctx)`.
2. `backoffEnsureLease(ctx)` retries forever because the Lease can never be created.
3. On `SIGTERM`, the pre-shutdown hook calls `controller.Stop()`.
4. `Stop()` blocks waiting for `reconcilingLock`.
5. The retry context is only canceled after pre-shutdown hooks return.
6. Pre-shutdown hooks cannot return because `Stop()` is blocked.

This is not specific to hostnames. Any permanent `ensureLease` failure can block shutdown the same way.

This appears to have been introduced by #134514, shipped in v1.35.0. It is present in v1.35.x and v1.36.x, and not present in v1.34.x.

Fix: #140241. With that fix applied, the same setup exits about 2 seconds after `SIGTERM`.

### What did you expect to happen?

`SIGTERM` should shut down `kube-apiserver` within seconds.

If the identity Lease cannot be created, the identity feature should be degraded, but apiserver shutdown should not be blocked.

### How can we reproduce it?

Option A: component-level test

Run the regression test from #140241:

```
    TestStopDoesNotBlockWhenLeaseCannotBeCreated
```

in:

```
    staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/apimachinery/lease/controller_test.go
```
Without the `controller.go` fix from that PR, `Stop()` never returns and the test times out after 30 seconds. With the fix, it passes quickly.

Option B: real binaries in containers

Adjust `arm64`/`amd64` as needed.

```
    mkdir repro && cd repro

    curl -sLo kube-apiserver https://dl.k8s.io/v1.36.2/bin/linux/arm64/kube-apiserver
    chmod +x kube-apiserver

    curl -sL https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/releases/download/v3.6.4/etcd-v3.6.4-linux-arm64.tar.gz \
      | tar xz --strip-components=1 etcd-v3.6.4-linux-arm64/etcd

    openssl genrsa -out sa.key 2048
    openssl rsa -in sa.key -pubout -out sa.pub

    cat > test.sh << 'EOF'
    #!/bin/bash

    /repro/etcd \
      --data-dir=/tmp/etcd \
      --listen-client-urls=http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      --advertise-client-urls=http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      >/tmp/etcd.log 2>&1 &

    sleep 3

    /repro/kube-apiserver \
      --etcd-servers=http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
      --cert-dir=/tmp/certs \
      --secure-port=6443 \
      --bind-address=127.0.0.1 \
      --advertise-address=$(hostname -i) \
      --authorization-mode=RBAC \
      --disable-admission-plugins=ServiceAccount \
      --service-cluster-ip-range=10.0.0.0/24 \
      --allow-privileged=true \
      --service-account-issuer=https://127.0.0.1:6443/ \
      --service-account-key-file=/repro/sa.pub \
      --service-account-signing-key-file=/repro/sa.key \
      >/tmp/apiserver.log 2>&1 &

    PID=$!

    sleep 20

    echo "lease errors: $(grep -c 'Failed to ensure lease exists' /tmp/apiserver.log)"

    kill -TERM $PID

    for i in $(seq 45); do
      kill -0 $PID 2>/dev/null || {
        echo "RESULT: exited ${i}s after SIGTERM"
        exit 0
      }
      sleep 1
    done

    echo "RESULT: STILL RUNNING 45s after SIGTERM"
    EOF
```

```
    docker run --rm --hostname "$(python3 -c "print('a'*61+'.lo')")" \
      -v "$PWD":/repro ubuntu:24.04 bash /repro/test.sh
```

Expected result with a 64-byte hostname:

```
    RESULT: STILL RUNNING 45s after SIGTERM
```

For comparison, a 63-byte hostname exits normally:

```
    docker run --rm --hostname "$(python3 -c "print('a'*60+'.lo')")" \
      -v "$PWD":/repro ubuntu:24.04 bash /repro/test.sh
```

Expected result:

    RESULT: exited 2s after SIGTERM

### Anything else we need to know?

This was found in Kubebuilder CI, which runs controller tests against real `kube-apiserver` and `etcd` binaries through controller-runtime envtest. Teardown sends `SIGTERM` and later `SIGKILL`; there is no kubelet or container runtime involved.

Public examples:

- macOS runner with a 68-byte hostname:
  https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubebuilder/actions/runs/28746565395/job/85238353306?pr=5836
- Ubuntu runner with hostname set to 64 bytes:
  https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubebuilder/actions/runs/28747687942/job/85241306371?pr=5836

This does not appear to be connection draining. There are no in-flight or watch requests, and no shutdown activity begins.

It also does not appear to be signal delivery. `etcd`, started the same way on the same host, exits in under a second on `SIGTERM`, and the hung apiserver handles `SIGQUIT` normally.

Full goroutine dumps and `-v=4` logs are available if helpful.

### Kubernetes version

Reproduced with official v1.35.0 and v1.36.2 release binaries.

Introduced in v1.35.0 by #134514.
Present in v1.35.x and v1.36.x.
Not present in v1.34.x.

### Cloud provider

None. Plain host processes on GitHub Actions runners and a laptop.

### OS version

Reproduced on macOS 15 arm64 and Ubuntu 24.04 amd64/arm64.

The deciding variable is hostname length, not OS. Linux caps hostnames at 64 bytes, so only a 64-byte hostname exceeds the 63-byte label value limit.

### Install tools

None. Official release binaries executed directly.

### Container runtime (CRI) and version

### What happened?

Discussion Thread in slack: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0409NGC1TK/p1782398632052059

This issue is originally reported by @liggitt 

> Looking at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139698, I was digging into consumable capacity policy range step validation more ... it looks like the validation and use is coercing the requested values and steps to integers before determining if max-min divides evenly by step, etc. Was that intended? I didn't see anything in the design or validation of min / max that required integer values

Currently, the step alignment logic evaluates quantities using resource.Quantity.Value(). Because .Value() automatically ceils any fractional metric to the next whole integer, fractional steps (such as 0.5 or 2.5 core allocations) lose precision. For example, if a Step of 0.5 is processed, it is evaluated as 1, causing step math to behave incorrectly and misalign requested allocations.

### What did you expect to happen?

The system should either explicitly disallow fractional quantities with clear documentation, or it should preserve fractional values during conversion.

We should either 
- keep integer-only constraints with Value() conversion but update the documentation to explicitly state that fractional quantities are not supported 
- or update the internal logic to preserve fractional precision with a reasonable performance tradeoff. For example, we can use resource.Quantity.MilliValue() to support milli-scale metrics (like millicores).

### What happened?

 ### Issue Overview
In recent testing, sig-cli tests are experiencing intermittent flakes. The actual tests are passing, but they are failing during setup (BeforeEach) or cleanup (DeferCleanup).

The failure manifests as an authentication drop: the ClientSet loses its authentication context between the test execution and the AfterEach cleanup, resulting in system:anonymous forbidden errors when attempting to create resources (like oauthclients) or delete resources (like namespaces).

### Root Cause Analysis
The issue stems from how the ClientSet is constructed and retained in test/e2e/framework/framework.go.

**The Bug**
The ClientSet is created from a local variable (config) rather than the persistently stored framework configuration (f.clientConfig).

**Local Scope Issue:** The local config variable goes out of scope after BeforeEach() completes.

**Shallow Copy Flaw: T**he ClientSet holds a shallow copy that points to structures potentially tied to that local stack frame or shared memory.

**Why it surfaced now (Kubernetes v1.36):** This bug has always existed but was previously masked by strong references in the TLS transport cache. Kubernetes v1.36 introduced active garbage collection.

**The Flake:** Because the failure depends on when the active Garbage Collector (GC) drops the transport memory (once the local variable's strong reference expires), the unauthenticated client defaults to system:anonymous. This makes it a flake rather than a consistent failure.

### The Code Defect
In test/e2e/framework/framework.go:BeforeEach() (lines 220-234):

**Current Code:**

Go
config, err := LoadConfig()  // Line 221 - local stack variable
config.QPS = f.Options.ClientQPS
config.Burst = f.Options.ClientBurst
// ...
f.clientConfig = rest.CopyConfig(config)  // Line 232 - shallow copy stored
f.ClientSet, err = clientset.NewForConfig(config)  // Line 233 - BUG: uses local 'config', not 'f.clientConfig'

### The Proposed Fix
Construct the ClientSet using the copied, persistent configuration storage (f.clientConfig) rather than the short-lived local stack variable. This ensures the framework maintains a strong reference to the configuration throughout the entire lifecycle of the test.

**Fixed Implementation:**

func (f *Framework) BeforeEach(ctx context.Context) {
    // Load config ONCE and store it
    config, err := LoadConfig()
    ExpectNoError(err)

    config.QPS = f.Options.ClientQPS
    config.Burst = f.Options.ClientBurst

    // Store a DEEP COPY (not shallow)
    f.clientConfig = rest.CopyConfig(config)

    // IMPORTANT: Use the stored copy, not the local variable
    f.ClientSet, err = clientset.NewForConfig(f.clientConfig)

    // Even if someone modifies kubeconfig file later,
    // f.ClientSet still has the original credentials in memory

items.body:
#### What happened?

`resource.Quantity.AsApproximateFloat64()` returns `NaN` for a quantity whose value is exactly zero but whose scale is large (roughly `|scale| >= 309`).

In `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go`, the function short-circuits only when `exponent == 0`, then returns `base * math.Pow10(exponent)`. For a zero value, `base` is `0` and `math.Pow10(scale)` overflows to `+Inf`, so it returns `0 * +Inf`, which is `NaN`.

#### What did you expect to happen?

A zero-valued quantity should approximate to `0` regardless of scale. The sibling `AsFloat64Slow()` returns `0` for the same input, and the two are meant to agree (their test tables are annotated to be kept in sync).

#### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
q := resource.NewScaledQuantity(0, 500) // value 0, scale 500
fmt.Println(q.AsApproximateFloat64())   // got NaN, want 0
```

Equivalently, a table row `{intQuantity(0, 500, DecimalSI), 0.0}` added to `TestQuantityAsApproximateFloat64` fails with "expected 0, got NaN", while the same row passes in `TestQuantityAsFloat64Slow`.

#### Anything else we need to know?

The result is `NaN` only for an exactly-zero value at a large scale. Non-zero values are unaffected (a tiny non-zero value that underflows still returns `0`, which is the documented approximate behavior).

#### Kubernetes version

master (the code is unchanged across released versions).

/kind bug

items.body:
### What happened?

`StreamWatcher.Stop()` can send a spurious `watch.Error` event to the result channel instead of closing it cleanly.

`Stop()` closes the HTTP response body via `source.Close()`, causing the blocked `Decode()` in `receive()` to fail with `"http2: read on closed response body"`. Since `IsProbableEOF` does not recognize this error string, `receive()` attempts to send the error as a `watch.Error` event.


### What did you expect to happen?

The `"http2: read on closed response body"` error should be treated as EOF.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start a watch against the API server
2. Read from `ResultChan()` in a consumer goroutine
3. Call `Stop()` from a separate goroutine while the consumer is still reading
4. Observe that ~50% of the time, the consumer receives a `watch.Error` event with message `"unable to decode an event from the watch stream: http2: response body closed\") has prevented the request from succeeding"` before the channel closes.

At this point, both `<-sw.done` and `sw.result <- Event{Error}` are ready in a `select`, and per the Go spec one is chosen at random — so roughly 50% of the time, a spurious error event is delivered to the consumer.

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
### What happened?

When reflector uses List+Watch, it request ANY version by setting RV=0. [Code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0cd4e13c69be9ec44267efeaf9acfd90ef4af5f5/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L1126-L1130)
When reflector uses WatchList, it always requests MostRecent version. [Code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0cd4e13c69be9ec44267efeaf9acfd90ef4af5f5/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L1135-L1144)

When the apiserver watch cache is temporarily falling behind (due to high load):
1. A controller with old ListWatch approach is more resilient to temporary staleness given it uses RV=0 .
2. A controller with WatchList with MostRecent semantic approach can suffer longer bootstrap time due to multiple attempts and timeouts. 

More details about the 2nd scenario:
1. Controller (e.g. KCM) initialize a WatchList request with MostRecent
2. APIServer queries etcd to get the latest RV=X
3. APIServer times out after waiting 3s and return 429 to client.
4. Controller retries another WatchList request with MostRecent
5. APIServer queries etcd to get the latest RV=Y (Y>X)
6. APIServer may already have X, but can't catch up with Y in 3s, it returns 429 to client
7. This repeats multiple rounds until the watch cache catches up. During this time, the controller can still hold the leadership because the lease update is cheap and always succeeds even when other resource watch cache is falling behind, but makes no progress for a couple minutes.


### What did you expect to happen?

From resilient to temporary staleness perspective, controller initialization using WatchList should not be worse than the old List+Watch behavior.

A few options to consider:
1. WatchList in Reflector use RV=0 instead of RV="". (easiest and matching old behavior)
2. WatchList can wait longer than 3s before giving up
3. Even when watch cache is not up to date, WatchList starts to serve synthetic events immediately from watch cache and dispatch new etcd events that apiserver receives until it catches up with RV=X. Then it sends the bookmark event. The initEvents no longer contain pure synthetic ADD events.
4. Everything is same as option 3 above except that WatchList starts to serve synthetic events from watch cache after waiting for up to 3s.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138728#issuecomment-4445545871 should be able to reproduce

items.title: Migrate 'Good First Migration' metav1.Condition Fields to Declarative Validation

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

This issue tracks a number of identified "good first migration" cases from handwritten Go code to Declarative Validation tags as part of KEP-5073. Following the initial migration of `metav1.Condition` in [PR 139101](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139101), this issue tracks migrating the remaining handwritten validations for the `Condition` struct fields. The goal is to easily aid the community in the migration by having a set of cases with minimal migration friction.

For more information on the tasks here, the Declarative Validation work group has open discussion in the Kubernetes Slack channel: `#sig-api-machinery-dev-tools`.

### IMPORTANT! - PR Structure

The ideal PR structure for contributing a DV tag migration is:
- **Commit # 1:** Use a single DV tag on a single field. E.g. Add `+k8s:alpha(since: "1.37")=+k8s:maxLength=1024` to a field. Includes updated tests in `test/declarative_validation/meta/conditions.go`.
- **Commits # 2...N:** Add more DV tags on the same field, one per commit; repeat until that field is done.
- **Commits N+1...M:** Repeat the above for other fields in your chosen batch.

The emphasis is on small commits. Maintaining commit discipline is hard but worthwhile.

### Resources

- **KEP:** [KEP-5073: Declarative Validation](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/5073-declarative-validation)
- **Reference PR:** [PR 139101](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139101) which set up `metav1.Condition` declarative validations.

### Task List

The following handwritten validations for `metav1.Condition` in `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/types.go` are candidates for migration. (Note: Each batch can be filed as a separate PR).

**If you are working on a batch, please comment on this issue with the batch number you are claiming to avoid duplicate work and conflicts.**

*Note: Some handwritten validations like `LastTransitionTime.IsZero()` and `Reason` pattern matching cannot currently be migrated since declarative validations do not support `+k8s:required` on non-pointer structs or generic regex patterns respectively.*

#### Batch 1: `Reason`
- [ ] `Reason`
  - Required (`+k8s:required`)
  - MaxLength 1024 (`+k8s:maxLength=1024`)

#### Batch 2: `Message`
- [ ] `Message`
  - Optional (`+k8s:optional`)
  - MaxLength 32768 (`+k8s:maxLength=32768`)

#### Batch 3: `Status`
- [x] `ConditionStatus` (Type) and `Status` (Field)
  - Enum (True, False, Unknown): Add `// +k8s:enum` to the `type ConditionStatus string` definition in `types.go`. This automatically enables enum validation for fields of this type.
  - Required (`+k8s:required`): Add this to the `Status` field inside the `Condition` struct. (Note: this will correctly standardize the error for a missing status to `Required` instead of `NotSupported`).

#### Batch 4: `Type` (Continuation)
- [ ] `Type`
  - Format `k8s-label-key` (`+k8s:format=k8s-label-key`)

#### Batch 5: `ObservedGeneration`
- [x] `ObservedGeneration`
  - Optional (`+k8s:optional`)
  - Minimum 0 (`+k8s:minimum=0`)

### How to Migrate a Field in `Condition`

1. **Locate the Type:** Find the `Condition` struct (or `ConditionStatus` type) in `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/types.go`.
2. **Add the Tag:** Add the corresponding declarative validation tags (e.g., `// +k8s:alpha(since: "1.37")=+k8s:maxLength=1024`) above the field or type definition.
3. **Generate:** Run `hack/update-codegen.sh validation`.
4. **Update Tests:** Update `GenerateConditionTestCases` in `test/declarative_validation/meta/conditions.go` to add new `ConditionTestCase` items that violate your new validation rules. This will automatically ensure that all API groups using `Conditions` run these test cases!
   - *Note: `test/declarative_validation/certificates/podcertificaterequest/declarative_validation_test.go` has its own custom testcases for `Conditions` (because its handwritten validation enforces specific condition types), so you must also add your test cases to the `testCases` array there.*
5. **Verify:**
   - Run tests: `make test WHAT=./test/declarative_validation/...`
6. **Mark Covered:** In the original handwritten validation in `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/validation/validation.go` (inside `ValidateCondition`), find the manual check and mark it with `.MarkCoveredByDeclarative()`.

**Example of marking hand-written validation code:**
```go
// For simple inline errors:
if condition.ObservedGeneration < 0 {
    allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Invalid(fldPath.Child("observedGeneration"), condition.ObservedGeneration, "must be greater than or equal to zero").MarkCoveredByDeclarative())
}

// For validation helpers returning ErrorList:
errs := ValidateLabelName(condition.Type, fldPath.Child("type"))
allErrs = append(allErrs, errs.MarkCoveredByDeclarative()...)
```

items.title: Clean up OptionalSlice validation interface to avoid using errors for control flow

labels.name: sig/api-machinery
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

labels.name: area/api-validation
labels.description: Issues or PRs related to API validation and declarative validation

items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
During the review of [PR #139101](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139101#discussion_r3306853033), reviewers noted that the implementation of `OptionalSlice` in declarative validation is highly confusing. 

The godoc explains that it returns an error when an optional value is not specified. However, returning an error in this scenario seems to contradict the idea that an optional value is allowed to be unspecified.

In the generated code, `OptionalSlice` is currently used exclusively for its side effect to check if it is safe to return early:

```go
if e := validate.OptionalSlice(ctx, op, fldPath, obj, oldObj).MarkAlpha().MarkShortCircuit(); len(e) != 0 {
	earlyReturn = true
}
```
Constructing an error at runtime only to use it for this side-effect is not ideal and needs to be improved.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Redesign the `OptionalSlice` validation interface (and related generated code) so that it doesn't rely on returning an `ErrorList` purely for early-return control flow. The interface should be clear and not treat a missing optional field as an error condition.

### What happened?

When sending a DELETE request with invalid JSON types for fields in `DeleteOptions`, the API Server returns HTTP 500.

For example, when `gracePeriodSeconds` is provided as a string instead of an integer, the API Server returns an internal server error:

```json
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "json: cannot unmarshal string into Go struct field DeleteOptions.gracePeriodSeconds of type int64",
  "code": 500
}
```

Similar HTTP 500 responses can also be triggered by invalid types in other `DeleteOptions` fields, such as `ignoreStoreReadErrorWithClusterBreakingPotential`, `orphanDependents`, `propagationPolicy`, and `preconditions`.

These errors are caused by malformed client input and should not be reported as internal server errors.

2. Start a local API proxy:
```bash
kubectl proxy --port=8001
```

```bash
curl -X DELETE 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/apis/admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1/validatingwebhookconfigurations' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
```

items.body:
### What happened?

**Issue 1**: GVR Resource string uses naïve pluralization

The new WithInformerName(gvr) code path in cmd/informer-gen/generators/informer.go hardcodes:
```
  "resourceName": strings.ToLower(t.Name.Name) + "s",
```
producing wrong plurals (blockaffinitys, globalnetworkpolicys, etc.) for any type whose API plural isn't + "s". 

This is inconsistent with the same generator's `generic.go`, which uses the `plural-exceptions-aware` namer:
```
  "resourceName": codegennamer.NewTagOverrideNamer(
      "resourceName", namer.NewAllLowercasePluralNamer(g.pluralExceptions),
  ),
```
The `--plural-exceptions` flag is already plumbed through informer-gen for generic.go. It just needs to feed informer.go's resourceName value too.

**Issue 2**: Godoc bugs in factory.go template
 - Variable name typo
```
  typedInformer := factory.SomeAPIGroup().V1().SomeType()
  handle, err := typeInformer.Informer().AddEventHandler(...)   // typeInformer ≠ typedInformer
```
Defined as typedInformer, referenced (twice) as typeInformer. Won't compile if copy-pasted.

- Self-referential deprecation guidance
```
  // WaitForCacheSync should be used instead of WaitForCacheSync in code which supports contextual logging.
```
Should be `WaitForCacheSyncWithContext should be used` instead of WaitForCacheSync ....

- Example ranges over a struct
```
  synced := factory.WaitForCacheSyncWithContext(ctx)
  for v := range synced { ... }
```

`WaitForCacheSyncWithContext` returns cache.SyncResult (a struct, not iterable). Won't compile.

All three are textual edits in the same template file.


### What did you expect to happen?

**Issue 1**: GVR Resource string uses naïve pluralization
Expected:
blockaffinity -> blockaffinites
globalnetworkpolicy -> globalnetworkpolicies

items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Currently, it is possible for API authors and reviewers to add Server-Side Apply (SSA) list tags (like `+listType=map`) and mistakenly assume they are fully declaring the validation, without realizing they also need to double-specify the Declarative Validation (DV) tags (like `+k8s:listType=map`).

This edge case can easily bite authors who might reasonably think that `+listType=map` alone makes the server enforce a unique map key.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
We should add a new rule, likely to the Kube API Linter (KAL), that catches new types and ensures they include the DV-triggering tags when `+listType` or `+listMapKey` are used.

Since adding DV tags to all existing fields would generate validation code that requires handwritten validation (HV) modifications and tests, a global enforcement might result in more exemptions than enforcements. Therefore, the linter should specifically target new groups, versions, or types to ensure we don't propagate this gap further.

**Related PRs/Issues:**
* Discovered and discussed in kubernetes/kubernetes#139101 (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139101#discussion_r3283550816)

items.body:
Follow-on to #139257. That issue tracked a compile error (`undefined: http2.TrailerPrefix`) introduced under Go tip = go1.27 by the x/net/http2 reshuffle in #139248, and was fixed by bumping to x/net v0.55.0 in #139258. With the build unblocked, a second defect from the same reshuffle is now visible: `ci-kubernetes-unit-golang-tip` is still red, with a different signature.

Multiple apiserver HTTP/2 tests fail with TLS ALPN errors:

```
http: TLS handshake error from 127.0.0.1:...: tls: client requested unsupported application protocols (["h2"])
authentication_test.go:685: Get "https://...": remote error: tls: no application protocol
```

Affected tests include `TestUnauthenticatedHTTP2ClientConnectionClose/*` (all subtests), `TestGracefulTerminationWithKeepListeningDuringGracefulTermination{Disabled,Enabled}`, `TestPreShutdownHooks/*`, `TestMuxAndDiscoveryComplete`, and `TestNew/non-nil_dial_holder+internal`, all in `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/{server,endpoints/filters}`.

Root cause is in vendored `golang.org/x/net@v0.55.0`. The package now splits its server into two implementations:

- `vendor/golang.org/x/net/http2/server.go` — build tag `!(go1.27 && !http2legacy)`. Its `configureServer` appends `"h2"` and `"http/1.1"` to `s.TLSConfig.NextProtos` at lines 205-209.
- `vendor/golang.org/x/net/http2/server_wrap.go` — build tag `go1.27 && !http2legacy`. Its `configureServer` at lines 26-56 does not touch `NextProtos` at all (and does not nil-init `TLSConfig` either).

Under Go tip (identifying as go1.27), `http2.ConfigureServer` therefore no longer registers the h2 ALPN protocol. Tests that use `httptest.Server.StartTLS()` after calling `http2.ConfigureServer` end up with an `http/1.1`-only ALPN list, and the TLS handshake rejects any client that requests h2 with `tls: no application protocol`. Production apiserver code paths that rely on `http2.ConfigureServer` to wire up ALPN are affected by the same defect, not just tests.

The regression boundary in this job:

- last green: build 2057884102870175744 at `45f714fc36` (2026-05-22T18:00:07Z)
- first red (compile error, fixed by #139258): build 2057944767483875328 at `0f935974ee` (2026-05-22T22:01:10Z)
- first red showing the ALPN failure (immediately after #139258 merged): build 2058186598851284992 at `6790dcf1f6` (2026-05-23T14:02:07Z)
- still red on current HEAD as of build 2058549996172611584 at `e09c6f3997` (2026-05-24T14:06:08Z)

The introducing change is PR #139248. Despite its title ("Bump golang.org/x/crypto to v0.52.0") it also re-vendored `golang.org/x/net/http2/` and brought in the `server_wrap.go`/`transport_wrap.go` go1.27 split that contains the defect.

Possible fixes, in order of preference:

1. Upstream `golang.org/x/net`: add the NextProtos append (and the `if s.TLSConfig == nil` guard) to `server_wrap.go`'s `configureServer` so the go1.27 path matches the legacy path. Then bump to the next x/net release in k8s.
2. Carry a local vendor patch on `vendor/golang.org/x/net/http2/server_wrap.go` (and matching staging modules) until upstream lands.
3. Build with `-tags http2legacy` for the golang-tip job to opt out of the wrapper path; not a fix, but unblocks CI.

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG API Machinery.
